person.name: Heinz_Nixdorf
person.summary: Heinz Nixdorf (1925–1986) was a German computer pioneer and entrepreneur who founded Nixdorf Computer AG and built it from a tiny start‑up into a major international electronics and computing company. Coming from a poor railway family and interrupted by wartime service, he fought his way back to complete secondary school, study applied physics, and gain crucial experience in calculator development at Remington Rand. With early backing from the utility RWE, he created Germany’s first tube‑based computer, then shifted to transistor and semiconductor technology, becoming a leading figure of the German Wirtschaftswunder and a key promoter of decentralized data processing and workforce training until his sudden death at a trade fair in 1986.

chapters.headline: Hardship Shaped Beginnings
chapters.description: Childhood in economically strained circumstances and the decisive break from a prescribed teaching career set the foundation for his independence and scientific interests.

chapters.headline: War Service To Scholarship
chapters.description: Military service, family loss and postwar responsibilities delay his education, but he ultimately secures the Abitur and embarks on physics studies while gaining key industry experience.

chapters.headline: Pioneering Impulse Technology
chapters.description: Abandoning university, he founds his own laboratory in Essen and develops Germany’s first tube‑based computer, transforming a small contract operation into a growing electronics firm.

chapters.headline: Rise As Small‑Computer Pioneer
chapters.description: After relocating to Paderborn, he steers his company toward semiconductor‑based small computers, launches the System 820, and consolidates activities into Nixdorf Computer AG as a full‑line manufacturer.

chapters.headline: Global Expansion Era
chapters.description: Building on his Paderborn base, he conquers international markets, enters the United States, expands a major high‑tech campus, and leads Nixdorf Computer AG to global prominence until his sudden death.

events.title: Birth in Paderborn
events.description: Heinz Nixdorf is born in Paderborn as the eldest of five children of railway employee Walter Nixdorf and his wife Änne. Shortly after his birth the family moves to Torgau in Saxony and does not return to Paderborn until 1931. His childhood is marked by his father’s intermittent unemployment and material poverty, which later shapes his emphasis on job creation as an entrepreneur.

events.title: Break from teacher track
events.description: Thanks to scholarships for his strong school performance, Nixdorf attends several teacher‑training colleges between 1939 and 1942, although he feels confined by the expectation that he will become a teacher. Against the wishes of his mother and teachers, he petitions the Prussian Ministry of Education in [[Berlin|Berlin]] in 1941 for permission to move to the [[Reismann‑Gymnasium|Reismann‑Gymnasium]] in Paderborn. When the ministry grants his request, he returns to a classical secondary‑school path and shows particular talent in mathematics and the natural sciences.

Berlin.explanation: At the time the capital of Prussia within Nazi Germany and seat of central ministries such as the Prussian Ministry of Education, which controlled schooling and teacher training.

Reismann\u2011Gymnasium.explanation: A traditional humanistic secondary school (Gymnasium) in Paderborn that offered a classical curriculum preparing students for the Abitur university entrance examination.

events.date_note: Covers wartime service from 1943 and completion of Abitur in 1947
events.title: War service and late Abitur
events.description: In 1943 Nixdorf is called up for [[Reichsarbeitsdienst|Reich Labour Service]] and then for training at a Luftwaffe school in the [[Weserbergland|Weserbergland]], where his sporting talent helps him gain several glider pilot licences. He joins the [[NSDAP|NSDAP]] in 1943 and later serves with the elite Panzer‑Division "Hermann Göring"; after its defeat in Bohemia he escapes capture and makes his way back to Paderborn in May 1945. With his father killed on the Eastern Front in 1944, the twenty‑year‑old must help support his widowed mother and siblings through farm work before he can complete his interrupted schooling. Only in 1947 is he able to sit for and pass the Abitur at the Reismann‑Gymnasium, opening the way to university study.

Reichsarbeitsdienst.explanation: The Reich Labour Service was a compulsory state labour organization in Nazi Germany that conscripted young men and women for paramilitary work and pre‑military training before or instead of regular military service.

Weserbergland.explanation: The Weserbergland is a hilly region along the middle course of the Weser River in northwestern Germany, used during World War II for various military training facilities due to its terrain.

NSDAP.explanation: The NSDAP (National Socialist German Workers' Party) was the fascist political party led by Adolf Hitler that ruled Germany from 1933 to 1945.

events.title: Studies and Remington Rand training
events.description: Supported by a scholarship, Nixdorf studies applied physics at Goethe University Frankfurt from 1947, supplementing his scientific work with seminars in business administration. In 1951 he becomes a working student in the development department of the German subsidiary of the American office‑machine firm Remington Rand. There he helps design simple counting devices and learns the basics of building electronic calculators, working closely with department head Walter Sprick. When Sprick leaves because Remington no longer supports his projects, he transfers his inventions and patent rights to Nixdorf, giving the young physicist a technological foundation for his own systems such as the Elektronensaldierer and Elektronenmultiplizierer.

events.title: Founds Labor für Impulstechnik
events.description: Convinced of the potential of electronic calculators based on [[vacuum tube|vacuum tubes]], Nixdorf pitches his ideas to major firms in [[North Rhine-Westphalia|North Rhine‑Westphalia]]. At the utility [[Rheinisch-Westfälische Elektrizitätswerk|Rheinisch‑Westfälische Elektrizitätswerk]] (RWE) in Essen he wins the backing of the head of the punched‑card department, who secures a 30,000‑mark development contract, underwritten personally by Walter Sprick. Nixdorf abandons his physics studies in the ninth semester and in 1952 founds the Heinz Nixdorf Labor für Impulstechnik (LFI) in the basement rooms of RWE’s administration building in Essen, soon hiring radio and television technician Alfred Wierzoich as his first employee.

vacuum tube.explanation: An early electronic component used to control electric current flow in devices such as radios and early computers before the widespread adoption of transistors.

North Rhine-Westphalia.explanation: A federal state in western Germany that became a major postwar industrial and technology region, home to many large utilities and manufacturers.

Rheinisch-Westf\u00e4lische Elektrizit\u.explanation: A large regional electric utility company in western Germany (now part of RWE AG) that played a key role in postwar industrial development.

events.title: Delivers first German tube computer
events.description: By early 1954 Nixdorf’s small team at the Labor für Impulstechnik delivers its first major product for RWE’s bookkeeping department, the ES, an electronic calculator based on [[vacuum tube|vacuum tubes]]. The machine processes data stored on punched cards and is regarded as the first tube‑based computer built in Germany. Rapid further developments follow, all installed at RWE, forcing Nixdorf already in 1954 to rent additional space near the utility and gradually loosen his firm’s dependence on this single customer.

images.caption: Logo Labor für Impulstechnik Heinz Nixdorf

vacuum tube.explanation: An early electronic component that controls electric current flow in a high‑vacuum sealed glass or metal envelope, used before transistors to build amplifiers, radios, and the first generations of computers.

events.title: Moves company to Paderborn
events.description: Seeking room for expansion and better cost structures, Nixdorf relocates his firm’s headquarters from Essen to his home town of Paderborn in 1959. The medium‑sized Westphalian city offers lower wage levels and a deep labour pool, allowing him to grow more flexibly than in the Ruhr. By 1961 he is already employing around 50 people there, transforming the former niche supplier into a rapidly expanding electronics manufacturer.

events.title: Presents Wanderer Logatronic
events.description: Facing order shortfalls from key customers such as Wanderer‑Werke and Bull, Nixdorf gambles on a new generation of compact computer. He recruits engineer Otto Müller, whose ideas for a desk‑top calculator he has noticed at the [[Hannover Messe|Hannover Messe]], and despite initial doubts eventually backs Müller’s concept. In 1965 the resulting Wanderer Logatronic is unveiled at the Hannover Messe: the first small computer constructed entirely with semiconductor technology and designed on modular principles, a technical revolution that lays the groundwork for a new product family.

Hannover Messe.explanation: An internationally significant industrial trade fair held annually in Hanover, Germany, where companies present new technologies and products.

events.title: Launches Nixdorf System 820
events.description: Building on the Logatronic, Nixdorf’s company develops the Nixdorf System 820, introduced from 1967 onwards as a universal small computer. The System 820 features a [[magnetic-core memory|magnetic‑core memory]], an integrated keyboard and a typewriter for output, and it is freely programmable, making it ideal for decentralized electronic data processing in medium‑sized firms. Produced under various brand names by partners such as Wanderer‑Werke, Kienzle‑Apparate and Ruf‑Buchhaltung, the system meets a clear market need and cements Nixdorf’s reputation as a pioneer of small‑scale computing. At the same time he begins building his own nationwide sales network, shifting his company from component supplier to full‑line computer manufacturer.

magnetic-core memory.explanation: A type of random-access computer memory that stores data using tiny magnetized ferrite rings (cores), widely used in computers from the 1950s to the early 1970s before being replaced by semiconductor memory.

events.date_note: April 1968 marks the majority share acquisition; the legal merger took effect on 1 October 1968
events.title: Creates Nixdorf Computer AG
events.description: In April 1968 Nixdorf acquires the majority of shares in Wanderer AG for eight million Deutschmarks, largely financed from retained earnings. On 1 October 1968 the former Wanderer‑Werke and the Labor für Impulstechnik are merged to form Nixdorf Computer AG with headquarters in Paderborn. Overnight, Nixdorf gains not only powerful development and production units but also a Germany‑wide sales and service network and valuable know‑how in fine‑mechanical and electromechanical technologies. The new stock company becomes the vehicle for his subsequent international expansion.

events.date_note: Covers expansion steps following the Wanderer takeover, including the Victor Comptometer deal and global sales build‑out
events.title: Breaks into U.S. market
events.description: After the Wanderer takeover, Nixdorf travels to the United States to scout opportunities and spots a neglected niche for mini‑computers in banks, supermarkets, industry and health insurance funds. The American office‑machine specialist Victor Comptometer in Chicago places a huge order for 10,000 "Conti" calculators worth about 100 million Deutschmarks, forcing Nixdorf to expand production capacity. He subsequently acquires Victor Comptometer, giving Nixdorf Computer its own American subsidiary and a foothold in a market dominated by U.S. giants such as IBM. By 1972 the company has built up a presence in 22 countries worldwide, transforming itself into a truly international electronics group.

events.title: Expands Paderborn technology campus
events.description: From 1974 onward Nixdorf systematically develops the Paderborn site into a modern high‑tech campus. Along the former Unterer Frankfurter Weg, later renamed Heinz‑Nixdorf‑Ring, new production plants and office buildings are erected almost every year to keep pace with booming demand. The complex becomes a visible symbol of Nixdorf Computer AG’s role in the German Wirtschaftswunder, and of Heinz Nixdorf’s belief in combining industrial growth with extensive in‑house training and further education for his workforce.

events.title: Sudden death at Hannover Messe
events.description: On 17 March 1986, during the [[CeBIT|Cebit computer fair]] held on the Hannover Messe grounds, Heinz Nixdorf dies unexpectedly while attending the event. His death shocks Germany’s computer industry, as he had been one of its most dynamic and visible entrepreneurial figures. Nixdorf Computer AG, by then a multi‑billion‑mark corporation with tens of thousands of employees worldwide, loses its founder at the height of its international success.

CeBIT.explanation: CeBIT (Centrum für Büroautomation, Informationstechnologie und Telekommunikation) was, from 1986 to 2018, one of the world’s largest trade fairs for information technology, held annually in Hanover, Germany.
